verdict.reasoning: Patient states diarrhea has been “about three days now” and goes “Four to five” times a day; denies blood (“No blood”) and mucus (“No, no”).
Patient describes “pretty standard diarrhea where there’s like a little bit of abdominal pain,” indicating mild pain.
Patient says, “I threw up once,” confirming a single episode of vomiting.
When asked about fever, patient responds, “Maybe a little bit, but it hasn’t been that in particular hasn’t been too worrying,” consistent with a slight low-grade fever.
Patient reports, “A little bit of appetite loss, I guess, versus the normal,” which describes mild loss of appetite.
Patient notes no recent travel or unusual food: “nothing funky in my diet or no travels recently” and confirms “no” to “anything from outside? Nothing dodgy”.
When asked if he is drinking plenty, patient confirms, “Yeah, yeah, yeah… Mostly to try and rid,” and clinician notes “you’re still drinking plenty,” indicating adequate fluid intake.
In past medical history, patient says, “Probably at asthma or. Or, I don’t know, I guess I still have it,” confirming asthma history.
Patient confirms using an inhaler and that it is yellow: “Are you using any inhalers at all? … Yes.” and later “Is it like a blue color? Doctor: Yellow.”

Patient names “Lexapro” in response to which inhaler he uses and the clinician expresses uncertainty: “Which ones? Doctor: Lexapro… Patient: Okay, not heard of it. Maybe is it like salbutamol?” indicating confusion about Lexapro as an inhaler.

After discussing the inhaler, clinician asks about other meds: “Any other medication that you’re using over the counter, Anything at all, regularly? No.” So no other OTC or regular meds besides the named product.
On allergies: “Any allergies? Doctor: Nothing. Yeah, nothing. Patient: No allergies at all.”
Patient states, “He died of bowel cancer 10 years ago… And how old was he when he died? 62.”
Patient says, “My dad had hypertension… Has hypertension? … Hypertension. Yeah.” which confirms a history of hypertension in the father.
Clinician remarks, “you’re still drinking plenty and you look like you’re not dehydrated, which is a good sign,” indicating observed non-dehydration.
Acute diarrhea is discussed but no explicit etiologic assessment (e.g., “viral” or “self-limited”) is stated in the transcript.
Asthma is noted in history but there is no statement in the transcript that asthma is “stable” or any assessment of its control.
Family history of bowel cancer is clearly documented: “He died of bowel cancer 10 years ago,” so including it in the assessment is consistent with the transcript.
Clinician advises, “soft diet, so avoid dairy, fish, meat, eggs while you’re having the diarrhea” and explains soft diet as “crackers, toast, jam, those kind of things that’s easily digestive.”

Clinician says, “Once you are able to, you know, keep most of it in, you can start off with some just boiled vegetables and mash. Once you’re okay with that for about 48 hours, then you can start having meat.” The 48 hours refers to tolerating vegetables/mash, not 48 hours without symptoms before starting them.

Transcript: “Once you’re okay with [boiled vegetables and mash] for about 48 hours, then you can start having meat… just don’t have meat immediately once you feel like you’re slightly better,” which matches introducing meat/fish/eggs only after sustained improvement.
Clinician advises, “although you can’t. Milk is not a good idea. Yogurts are a good idea because they are probiotics. It help to build up the normal gut bacteria back.”

Clinician emphasizes hydration and ORS: “You still need to drink plenty of water because you’re losing a lot of fluids… you could get something called Di Rolite over the counter. So it helps to replenish the salts that you’ve been… lost through going to the toilet.”

Clinician says, “Things to look out for if your diarrhea doesn’t go away in a week’s time or if you’re passing blood. We need a stool sample,” and separately, “When we start worrying about diarrhea is if you’re going more than eight times a day,” but does not state obtaining stool studies specifically when >8 stools/day; that threshold is tied to dehydration/hospital, not ordering stool tests.

Clinician notes, “if you’re going about six to eight times a day, that means there’s a high chance that you are having dehydration and you might need to go into hospital at that point in time. If that happens, do get in touch with us again,” which instructs urgent re-evaluation with worsening dehydration or stool frequency 6–8/day.

Follow-up advice: “if your diarrhea doesn’t go away in a week’s time… do get in touch with us again” and “If that happens, do get in touch with us again,” covers persistence beyond a week or clinical deterioration.
